newsitem.title: UK: London bids Hong Kong farewell with low-key events.
newsitem.headline: London bids Hong Kong farewell with low-key events.

text.p: London greeted the handover of Hong Kong with a mixture of indifference and resigned acceptance on Monday, watching from afar as 156 years of British rule ended in tears of farewell in the rain.
On a grey day in the capital, there was little emotion as another small chunk dropped off the British empire, now reduced to a few scattered remnants.
While the media covered the event at length, with live television of events in Hong Kong since dawn, the general public appeared mildly interested but little moved.
In London's Chinatown, nestled in the heart of the West-End theatre district, a video-wall beaming live coverage from Hong Kong was the only intrusion into an otherwise normal day of business.
K.H. Wu, secretary of the Chinatown Chinese Association, said there would be no dragon dances, fireworks or overt celebration in Chinatown to mark the handover.
"The sole purpose of today is to let Chinese and foreigners alike know what is happening in Hong Kong," said Wu, a former civil servant in Hong Kong.
"We want to let the younger generation know why Hong kong is being handed back and why it was taken in the first place."

The political elite -- Prime Minister Tony Blair, other party leaders and ex-prime ministers -- was in the colony and parliament carried on its business with little regard to the moment of history occurring thousands of kilometres to the east.
"My mood is commiseration rather than celebration," said Hong Kong Chinese travel agent Bob Hawkett, as he sipped his jasmine tea.
"People in Hong Kong are still worried about communism. They're worried that further down the line China will try to impose its own laws on Hong Kong," Hawkett said.
"But they know that as long as they keep their noses clean and keep themselves to themselves, they'll get by."
Opinions on the political fate of Hong Kong were divided, but most people in Chinatown saw the arrival of 4,000 People's Liberation Army troops after the handover was a necessity, not a threat.
"Sure it's a show of Chinese pride, but it's also practical," said 18-year-old student Mae Li, who took advantage of the five-day national holiday in Hong Kong to visit Britain.
"The British troops are leaving, and to keep law and order something needs to replace them," Li said.

"I'm prepared to adapt myself to the political changes and restrictions and freedom of speech in Hong kong, because I don't think there'll be a dramatic change after the handover. These celebrations are symbolic."

Events marking the handover were low-key across the capital. The media called the handover the biggest Chinese takeaway in history, and in the docklands of east London, a three-day festival of Chinese arts was reaching its climax ahead of China taking control of Hong Kong at a 1600 GMT ceremony.

Lion dances, dragon races and a pageant on stilts were performed in the London Arena which had been decorated to resemble Hong Kong's famous thoroughfare, Temple Street. The dock outside was modelled on Aberdeen harbour, home to the colony's floating restaurants.
The Hong Kong Society, grouping Britons who loved the bustle and money-making free market of Hong Kong, gathered at Sandown Park, a famous racecourse south of the capital.
After watching the handover ceremony, and cocktails and entertainment by a band from the Brigade of Gurkhas, the 2,000 guests will adjourn for a "western-style" dinner to chew over old times.
The Chinese embassy will mark the return of Hong Kong with a reception this evening for politicians, businessmen and media guests, mostly British.

Outside the embassy a vigil will be held by the Free Tibet Campaign, calling for the end of what protestors claim is China's colonial rule in Tibet. The handover will be marked by the banging of gongs outside the embassy.

"It is illegal to say "Free Tibet" in Tibet. As of today it will become illegal to say "Free Tibet" in Hong Kong," said member of parliament George Stevenson, chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group for Tibet.
"I'll go back to Hong Kong after the handover, sure I will, but I'll choose my timing very carefully," Hawkett said.
But Hawkett wasn't referring to any political risk.
"Once you get used to the climate here in Britain, Hong Kong's humidity is murder," he said, shivering as he looked up at London's drizzling skies.
